P1a: Experimenting with a different rule doesn't have to mean everybody goes out and buys new land right away. Try it inside the parent group first, then as a semi-autonomous project, and then, if it needs more independence, as a seed group nearby that still shares some tools, childcare, business or friendships. Splitting off completely should be just one step along that gradient, and nobody should have to do it just to be allowed to experiment.
P2a: But some experiments can't be tested cheaply. A different land system, a different population size, or a set of rules that support each other may look bad if it's starved of what it actually needs. "We tried it in one room for three months" isn't always a fair test.
P3a: If these communities are supposed to spread, at some point somebody has to solve the boring problem of how they stay connected without building another state. I don't want one super-commune with a nicer logo. I'd like communities that can help each other out and move people and knowledge around, and that stay different enough to keep learning from each other.
P4a: Once you get to the scale of a federation, that outward purpose gets concrete. It means spreading healing practices, training people and seeding new projects. And it means making sure no one comfortable enclave starts to think it's the whole movement.
P5a: The Federation of Egalitarian Communities says it's currently rebuilding, and that's a useful warning. Running a federation takes real work. Delegates, records, compliance, coordinating resources, meetings, succession, and whatever dispute function it actually takes on all use up labor and material capacity before local crises have eaten both. Where the legal or economic system around it requires money, the federation also needs a budget of outside cash. That work doesn't all have to sit in one body, though. Friendships between pairs of communities can exist alongside a general federation, and so can local clusters and institutions built around one function. The FEC's PEACH health pool, for example, is currently governed separately from the FEC's delegates.
P5e: The Federation of Egalitarian Communities is rebuilding right now, by its own account, which is a useful warning. A federation, like any institution, takes work. Delegates, records, compliance, resource coordination, meetings, succession, and whatever dispute function it actually accepts will soak up labor and material resources from the communities before local crises have eaten both. If the surrounding legal or economic system demands money, the federation will also need a budget of outside cash. It may be that not all of this work has to live under one roof: friendships between two communities, local clusters, and institutions that handle one specific function can coexist with a general federation. The FEC's current health pool, PEACH, for instance, is governed separately from the FEC delegates.
P6a: Cooperation also shouldn't quietly turn into assimilation. The FEC currently has full members and communities working toward membership, and it also has Friends who may just stay friends. People need the same kind of practical freedom between communities. If someone can move in theory, but their housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes and transition disputes all fall through the cracks, that freedom is just decoration. Often the answer is a thin interface that says who's responsible for what while somebody's crossing between them, without making every internal system match.
P6e: Cooperation also shouldn't quietly become assimilation. Right now the FEC allows for different kinds of relationship: full membership, working towards membership, or being a Friend of the FEC, which can stay just that. People need a similarly practical freedom between communities. If someone can move in theory, but their housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes and transition disputes fall into the cracks, the freedom is only decorative. Often the internal systems of different communities don't need to be made the same, they just need a thin interface that says who is responsible for what while somebody crosses between them.
P7a: Exchanges and obligations need the same honesty, even if nobody uses money internally. A gift of food, pooled medicine, lending a vehicle or a tool, trading labor, emergency housing, building something together, a visit that's mostly for training or building relationships: these are different events. Some of them create a future obligation and some don't. A federation can keep records for each purpose without putting a price on everything or forcing every transfer to come out even. If cash gets used where the federation meets the outside world, grants, loans, guarantees and shared-enterprise commitments need to be kept separate the same way. Solidarity doesn't mean unlimited joint liability, or an unlimited claim on another community's labor, stores, land or tools.
P7e: Exchange and obligations need the same honesty even if there's no money used internally. When somebody gives food as a gift, pools medicine, lends a vehicle or a tool, trades labor, offers emergency housing, works on a shared building project, or visits mainly for training or relationship building, those are different events. Some create a future obligation and some don't. A federation can keep purpose-specific records without putting a price on everything or forcing every transfer into parity. If cash is used at the interface with the outside, grants, loans, guarantees, and shared-enterprise commitments need to be kept apart the same way. Solidarity doesn't mean unlimited joint liability, and it doesn't mean an unlimited claim on another community's labor, stores, land, or tools.
P8a: And when two principles collide, don't just save the final rule. Keep the hard case too: what happened, which principles actually conflicted, what the first judgments were, the reasoning behind the final one, any dissent, what the consequences were, and exactly which version of the rule it was. When the rule changes, run the case again. Otherwise every generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
